svg.text: Two primary users and their jobs to be done · a six-group screen inventory with the grouping logic stated · three annotated flows, each with decision points, an unhappy path, and the law behind the decision.
Jobs trace to UX-02 (F-1–F-8). Laws of UX names follow lawsofux.com. IA principles follow the NN/g Information Architecture Study Guide, nngroup.com/articles/ia-study-guide/.
1 · Who this is for, and the job to be done
2 primary users · 3 jobs to be done
Five medications: three scheduled, two as-needed. Employer unnamed. Gender is not stated in the source, so this is written neutral. No diagnosis is added.
When my shifts rotate and I am the only one keeping track, I want one screen
that shows what is already done before it shows me what is next, so I can stop
Traces to: F-1 the record is half the product · F-3 interface depth is an accessibility problem · F-2 scheduling arithmetic is where products break
Rowan comes from the corrected persona pack. Nothing about Rowan is invented here; the pack and its
verification log are the source of record. Evidence for the job, not for the person:
GeekyDragonfly 05/04/2022, Meinnm505 May 5, rlsmith1994 Jun 9, tuxedoyam 12/25/2021,
SF Cavendish 11/23/2021. The interviews/ corpus is SIMULATED and is not evidence for this brief.
No job title, no diagnosis, no gender: the verification log retracted all three (C-05, C-06).
A person, not a market segment: 22 self-selected reviews are 22 people, not a rate.
Sourced only to UX-02 reviews. No name, age, job or diagnosis is invented, because nothing in the evidence base supplies one.
When my spouse and I both look after the same routine, I want a dose marked on
either phone to stop the reminder on the other, so I stop getting alarms for
something that has already been handled.
Traces to: F-4 and F-7 reminder persistence means opposite things depending on how many people share the record · F-5 reliability defects are trust defects
“My husband will mark something taken, I’ll get reminders on my device, and log in and see they’re already marked.”
123334567, App Store 08/06/2024 — the same mechanic is a feature for one reviewer and a fault for another
Feature side: rlsmith1994 Jun 9, eventidephoenix 10/10/2018 — “make it more annoying”.
This is why reminder escalation branches on the number of writers, not on a preference setting.
Deliberately unnamed. The corpus has no shared-household persona: Ada and Ray are two
separate people, not a couple, so neither was available to fill this role.
25 screens in 6 groups · max 2 taps from Today · 3 tabs + utility
not a tab · linear · every step skippable
S1 Welcome and what DoseDay does
S3 Notification rationale, then the OS prompt
S4 Reminder style: only me / someone helps
S5a Invite a carer → S5b Access level
E1 Empty state: Today with zero medicines
S4 is the highest-leverage question in the product. It is also the only
conditional branch in the whole spine, so it is the only fork drawn in Flow 2.
S10 As-needed dose logger (logs, never nags)
S11 Why didn’t I get a reminder? · RECOVERY
Order inside Today is the record first and the next action second (F-1), so the
first thing on screen answers “what is already done” rather than starting a countdown.
S8 is one of the five frames already on page 2. S9–S11 are
planned but not yet drawn at high fidelity.
S11 lives on Today, not in a help centre: recovery sits next to the thing that
failed, so it is found by tapping the row that failed.
S13 Add Medicine · amount and frequency · DESIGNED
S13 is where F-2 is designed in: “1 or 2 tablets”, 2-hourly, food-relative,
1×week to 3×/day and weekend-only all have to be expressible, because that is
where SF Cavendish and MikeyBGr8 gave up on a competitor.
Adding a medicine can never be blocked (F-5). CoastieWife74 lost a paid
subscription over exactly this, and nearly churned.
S19 Export and share with a clinician
No streaks, no scores, no red-for-missed. A missed dose is a reversible
check-in. This is a design constraint with zero user evidence behind it,
and it is recorded as such rather than dressed up as a finding.
S19 exists because a shareable summary for a doctor is a feature users named
as a reason to trust a competitor, not because the evidence priced it.
S17 is the fifth frame already on page 2.
S20 People and access: invite, remove, level
S21 Activity log: who marked what, and when
Most apps are single-writer, so a shared-care tab would be an empty tab for
almost every user. It is instead reached from Today, from a medicine, and
from Settings, and shown inline wherever a second writer matters.
S21 exists because 123334567’s complaint is not that reminders
kept firing, it is that the record looked wrong on the other phone.
Polyhierarchy, not duplication: one screen, three entry points.
S22 Reminder style and quiet hours
S23 Notification troubleshooting · deep link from S11
S24 Accessibility: text size, contrast, reduced motion
S25 Backup, export and delete all data
S22 is where the S4 fork can be changed later, so a wrong first answer is
S23 is the deepest screen in the product at 3 taps, and it is reached by
following a problem, never by browsing.
G1 · Three tabs, plus utility. Today, Medicines, Progress. Settings is utility navigation, not a peer tab. NN/g, Top 3 IA Questions about Navigation Menus, and NN/g, Utility Navigation.

G2 · No hamburger, ever. All top-level destinations are always visible. NN/g, Hamburger Menus and Hidden Navigation Hurt UX Metrics. F-3 is specifically a complaint about interface depth, so hiding navigation would contradict the finding.

G3 · Shallow, but not flattened. Two taps from Today to anything. NN/g, Flat vs. Deep hierarchies. I did not collapse everything into one screen either: NN/g, The 3-Click Rule for Navigation Is False, so depth is not a sin by itself and S23 is allowed to sit at 3 taps.

G4 · Grouped by user goal, not by database object. “Medicines”, not “Medication schedule entries”. NN/g, Information Scent: How Users Decide Where to Go Next, and the 4 Ss of link labelling. Labels carry the scent of the destination.

G5 · As-needed doses are an outlier, handled by cross-listing. The medicine lives in Medicines; the act of logging lives on Today. One object, two legitimate homes, no duplicate records. NN/g, How to Handle Category Outliers in Your IA, and Polyhierarchy.

G6 · Recovery lives next to the failure. S11 is reached from the row that failed, not from a help centre. Shared care is polyhierarchical, not a tab. NN/g, Navigation: You Are Here, and Local Navigation as an orientation aid.
Not validated by a card sort or a tree test. Both need participants, and the evidence base here is 22 self-selected reviews. The grouping is argued from evidence and stated openly as unvalidated.
each flow: decision points marked D1..Dn · at least one unhappy path · laws named at the decision
FLOW 1 · PRIMARY TASK — LOG A DOSE AND KNOW IT IS LOGGED
User 1 Rowan · traces to F-1 · 2 decision points · 1 unhappy path
Goal state: the user never has to remember whether a dose happened. The record answers it.
UNHAPPY PATH · WRONG DOSE, OR THE UNDO WINDOW CLOSED
A wrong entry is never a dead end: the log stays editable after the fact, so the 8-second undo is a convenience rather than the only way back.
LAWS BEHIND THESE DECISIONS · LAWS OF UX, LAWSOFUX.COM

D1 · Hick’s Law, Paradox of Choice. Two destinations, both one tap from the same row. No third option and no “more” menu. The amount for an as-needed dose is asked on the confirmation, not by adding a mode switch.

D2 · Undo, Recognition Rather Than Recall. The dose list is always on screen, so the user confirms by reading rather than by recalling. The 8-second undo exists so a mistake costs nothing, which is what makes people willing to tap at all.

Confirm · Doherty Threshold. The row updates immediately, so the wait never breaks the thought. Von Restorff. Today’s one outstanding row is the only visually distinct thing on screen, so it is the one that gets acted on.
Confirm · Peak-End Rule. The confirmation is the emotional end of the interaction, so it is warm, it is brief, and it is never red. A missed or corrected dose is not a failure state.
Traced to F-1: the record is half the product. Flow 1 is the whole product for Rowan, which is why it gets the shortest path and the most forgiving error handling.
Both users · traces to F-2, F-4 · 3 decision points · 2 unhappy paths
Goal state: the user lands on a working Today screen, not a form. Every step can be skipped and revisited in Settings.
UNHAPPY PATH A · NOTIFICATIONS REFUSED, AND A CARER NEVER INVITED
If an invite is sent but never accepted, the record stays single-writer and the reminder
style reverts to “only me”. A silent escalation is treated as a bug, not a preference: an
unanswered invite must never leave two people each assuming the other is dosing.
Refusing notifications costs the user reminders, not the app. The consequence is stated in one sentence before the OS prompt, and the product stays fully usable without push.
UNHAPPY PATH B · THE USER ABANDONS SETUP, OR SKIPS THE FIRST MEDICINE
Partly finished setup is kept: abandoning at S6 resumes at S6, not at S1, so someone who got two thirds of the way through is not made to start over.

Peak-End Rule the run ends on a working Today screen, not on a confirmation. Paradox of Choice two reminder styles, not a settings matrix. Chunking one decision per screen. Goal-Gradient Effect a visible step count, so the end is visibly near.

Zeigarnik Effect partial progress persists across an abandoned run. Signal the rationale is shown before the OS prompt, not after it. Constraints notification permission is the only hard gate, and it is bypassable.
Endowment Effect by the end they own a real medication entered in their own hand. Affordance “skip” is visible on the screen, not buried in a menu.
FLOW 3 · RECOVERY — THE REMINDER NEVER ARRIVED
Both users · traces to F-5 · 3 decision points · 1 unhappy path
Goal state: the user can always explain why a reminder did not arrive, and can still log the dose either way.
UNHAPPY PATH · NO CAUSE FOUND, AND THE DOSE IS ALREADY LATE
A missing reminder never blocks a dose. The manual log is always available, because from the user’s side
“the app is broken” and “the reminder never arrived” are indistinguishable — and we cannot tell them apart either.
CoastieWife74, a paid long-time user who could not add a medicine: “I don’t want to find a new app, but if this can’t be resolved, I’ll have to.”
Recovery is retention. The same person is why adding a medicine can never be blocked, and why this flow ends in a working log rather than a support ticket.

Help Users Recover from Errors the state is named in plain words and one concrete next step is offered: no error code, no blame, no dead end. Signal “expected 08:00, not logged” is a neutral signal rather than a red scolding.

Recognition Rather Than Recall the checklist is displayed, so nothing has to be remembered or guessed at. Layering one diagnostic surface, revealed progressively. Redundancy the manual log stands alone if every automatic path fails.

Undo a late entry stays correctable. Hick’s Law binary questions, asked one at a time. Doherty Threshold the test reminder gives immediate feedback. Processing Fluency short sentences and concrete nouns.
D1 exists because a genuine second writer is the most likely innocent explanation, and 123334567 experienced
it as a fault rather than as intended behaviour. Getting this wrong is how a correct feature becomes a bug report.
4 · What this page does not claim
• The IA was not validated by a card sort or a tree test. Both need participants; the base is 22 reviews.
• Screen count is a design intention, not a finding. 25 screens is what I intend to design, and all are listed.
• JTBD statements are written from review evidence about other products. None is a DoseDay user quote.
• User 2 is an archetype from one review thread, not a validated persona. It is deliberately unnamed.
• No wireframes here. Low-fidelity frames live on page 2; this page is structure only.
• No accessibility compliance claim is made from 22 reviews. PMC5694345 is corroboration, not a test.
A peer should be able to follow all three flows without me explaining them. If a step is not on this
page, it is not in the product yet.
LAWS OF UX · THE ONES ACTUALLY USED
Hick’s Law · Fitts’s Law · Jakob’s Law · Affordance · Signifier
Recognition Rather Than Recall · Law of Proximity · Law of Common Region
Peak-End Rule · Von Restorff (Isolation Effect) · Aesthetic-Usability Effect
Doherty Threshold · Undo · Help Users Recover from Errors · Constraints
Paradox of Choice · Chunking · Goal-Gradient Effect · Zeigarnik Effect
Layering · Redundancy · Endowment Effect · Processing Fluency
Streak — named only so it can be rejected
Law names as published on lawsofux.com. The Streak entry is deliberate: MyTherapy advertises
streaks as a headline benefit and no reviewer in the set mentions them either way, so the product
declines the mechanic rather than claiming evidence for refusing it.
